title: The Filter I Actually Use
description: What decides whether a traditional practice makes it onto Junoon, and what gets left out.
content:
People ask why Junoon only teaches some of what's technically "traditional" and skips the rest. Here's the actual filter: does it still do something when you take the ritual off it?

Dinacharya is a good test case. Charaka's daily routine gets flattened into a "morning routine" trend online: wake up early, drink water, journal. But his actual argument was narrower and more useful. Your body runs its own internal clock, and working with that clock instead of against it is most of what determines whether your day runs well or badly. That's not a lifestyle aesthetic. That's a claim about physiology, and it's one that circadian research backs up almost exactly.

Compare that to something like specific auspicious timings for practice, which shows up in some texts and doesn't survive the same question. I don't teach that here, not because it isn't old enough, but because nothing about it does anything when you check.

So when a practice is on Junoon, it earned its spot the same way: named tradition, named mechanism, and a reason that holds up outside the reverence. That's the whole standard.
